sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive (AR) language models by letting a small model draft tokens serially and a large model verify them in parallel. We reverse these roles. Starting from a standard AR checkpoint, we fine-tune the large model into a proposer that predicts a block of future tokens in a single forward pass, then use one additional forward pass to verify the proposed block. This gives ProVe, Proposer-Verifier decoding. The verifier can be a smaller AR model or the proposer itself; the latter gives ProVe-lossless, which reproduces the proposer's greedy AR decoding. Block proposals already provide substantial room for acceleration: with a block size of 16, the proposed block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens on GSM8K. Across six benchmarks with a 32B proposer, ProVe-lossless reaches 2.5x average AR throughput without training a separate draft head. With a small 3B verifier, ProVe reaches 2.7x average throughput at 2.6 accuracy points below AR on the six-task average, providing a controllable tradeoff between speed and accuracy.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive (AR) language models by letting small model draft tokens serially and large model verify them in parallel. We reverse these roles. Starting from standard AR checkpoint, we fine-tune the large model into proposer that predicts block of future tokens in single forward pass, then use one additional forward pass to verify the proposed block. This gives ProVe, proposer-verifier decoding. The verifier can be smaller AR model or the proposer itself; the latter gives ProVe-lossless, which reproduces the proposers greedy AR decoding. Block proposals already provide substantial room for acceleration: with block size of 16, the proposed block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens on GSM8K. Across six benchmarks with 32B proposer, ProVe-lossless reaches 2.5 average AR throughput without training separate draft head. With small 3B verifier, ProVe reaches 2.7 average throughput at 2.6 accuracy points below AR on the six-task average, providing controllable tradeoff between speed and accuracy. Figure 1. Three ways to spend two model calls per decoding cycle. (a) Speculative decoding: small model drafts one token per pass and the large model verifies the chain in one pass. (b) ProVe: the large proposer writes proposed block of 𝐵 tokens in one pass, and small verifier reads it in one more and commits the accepted prefix. (c) ProVe-lossless: the proposer verifies its own proposed block; the committed prefix plus its correction token equals greedy AR decoding, token for token.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Autoregressive (AR) language models produce one token per forward pass: response takes as many serial forward passes as it has tokens. Speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) cuts the number of passes of the large model by adding small model. small draft model proposes sequence of tokens, one at time. The large target model scores the sequence in one forward pass and keeps the proposed tokens up to the first one it disagrees with. The gain is set by how well the small model predicts the large one. Yet the draft model has to be much smaller than the target for its serial passes to be cheap. The roles are thus fixed by cost: drafting is serial, so it goes to the cheap model; verifying is one pass, so it goes to the expensive one. We ask whether the usual assignment of roles is still necessary once the large model can propose multiple tokens in single forward pass. MARS (Jin et al., 2026) provides exactly this capability: starting from an Nanyang Technological University. ByteDance. sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: ordinary AR checkpoint, it fine-tunes the model into block proposer that predicts the next 𝐵 tokens in one causal forward pass. The first proposed token is exactly the models ordinary next-token prediction, while later positions are predicted without access to the intervening future tokens (Section 2). Proposal quality decreases with depth in practice (Figure 3), but the key systems consequence is that proposal is no longer chain of 𝐵 serial model calls. This changes the role assignment itself. Once the large model can produce candidate block in one pass, the small model no longer has to spend serial steps drafting it; instead, it can read the realized block once and judge how much to keep. This gives ProVe, Proposer-Verifier decoding (Figure 2): the large block-proposing model proposes, and verifier reads the proposed block in second pass before deciding how much of it to commit. In the default ProVe setting, smaller AR model serves as the verifier. In ProVe-lossless, the proposer verifies its own block, so the resulting sequence reproduces the proposers greedy AR decoding. Both variants replace many serial AR steps with exact two forward passes per decoding cycle. Why pay for verifier when proposer confidence is already available for free? MARS commits from the same proposed block using the proposers own confidence, requiring no additional model pass. This gives controlled comparison: the proposer, the candidate block, and its confidence are held fixed, and ProVe changes only what happens after the block has been proposed. We find that the free confidence rule leaves much of the usable prefix uncommitted: along greedy continuations of GSM8K problems, the proposed block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens, while the default confidence rule commits only 3.0. Lowering the confidence threshold commits more tokens, but also increases the rate of committing tokens that diverge from greedy AR decoding (Section 3.1). The central question is therefore whether one additional verification pass can recover enough of this unused prefix to repay its cost. We evaluate ProVe and ProVe-lossless with 32B instruction proposer over six benchmarks and with 32B reasoning proposer (Section 4). ProVe-lossless reproduces the proposers greedy AR decoding and reaches 2.5 AR throughput on average, ranging from 1.4 on short constrained text to 4.0 on templated chains of thought. It outperforms public EAGLE-3 head and nearly matches head fine-tuned specifically for the proposer, without training separate draft head. With smaller verifier, ProVe provides controllable speedaccuracy tradeoff: 7B verifier reaches 2.3 average throughput with mean accuracy within 0.3 points of AR, while 3B verifier reaches 2.7 at 2.6 points below AR.

sections.title: Contributions
sections.content: Building on the block-proposing capability of MARS, we reverse the usual speculative-decoding roles: the large model proposes 𝐵 tokens in one pass, and verifier reads the realized block in one more. The verifier can be smaller AR model or, in ProVe-lossless, the proposer itself (Section 3). We isolate the value of verification with controlled comparison to the original MARS decoding rule: the proposer and proposed block are identical, while the confidence-only rule is free and ProVe deliberately pays one additional pass to read the realized trajectory. On GSM8K, the block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens, while the default confidence rule commits only 3.0 (Section 3.1). At 32B scale, ProVe-lossless reproduces the proposers greedy AR decoding at 2.5 average throughput without separate draft head, while smaller verifiers provide tunable speedaccuracy tradeoff reaching 2.7 average throughput with 3B verifier (Section 4.1). 2 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

sections.title: 2 Preliminaries: Block-Proposing AR Models

The asymmetry across positions is important. For 𝑖 = 1, no future token is missing from the conditioning context. For 𝑖 = 2, the proposer predicts one step further without seeing the token at position 𝑡 + 1; for larger 𝑖, progressively more intervening future tokens are replaced by placeholders. As Figure 3 shows, proposals are most reliable near the beginning of the block and become less reliable with depth in practice. Training. Following MARS (Jin et al., 2026), training combines the ordinary next-token objective with block-prediction objective on placeholder-corrupted responses. The former preserves ordinary AR generation, while the latter teaches the model to predict multiple future tokens in one pass. Importantly, block proposal does not introduce separate draft network or prediction head: ordinary AR prediction and block prediction use the same transformer and output head. The placeholders only provide the input pattern on which the model learns to predict farther into the future. Full training details are given in Appendix A. Original decoding rule. MARS uses the proposers own confidence to decide how much of each block to commit. It always commits the first proposed token, then continues from left to right while the confidence remains above threshold 𝜏. The committed prefix is appended to the context, and the proposer generates fresh block from the new position. Thus, each cycle uses one forward pass and commits between one and 𝐵 tokens. Section 3.1 examines how much of the proposed block this confidence rule is able to use. 3 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

sections.title: 3 Proposer-Verifier Decoding
sections.content: We take the MARS block proposer as fixed and change what happens after it produces block. The original MARS rule commits from the proposers confidence, which is already available from the proposal pass. ProVe deliberately spends one additional forward pass so that verifier can read the realized proposed tokens themselves before deciding how much to commit. This makes MARS particularly clean control: the proposer and candidate block are unchanged, and the only new computation is verification. We first ask whether this extra pass provides information worth paying for, then describe two choices of verifier.

sections.title: 3.1 Why Verify the Proposed Block?
sections.content: A block proposal is useful until it first diverges from the proposers greedy AR continuation. To measure how much useful content the proposer already produces, we run it along its own greedy continuations on randomly selected 300 GSM8K problems and propose block of 16 tokens at every position. We compare each proposed block with the continuation obtained by token-by-token greedy decoding. The average AR-matching prefix is 6.6 tokens. The original MARS rule is strong baseline precisely because its confidence signal is free: 𝑝𝑖 is produced by the same forward pass that produces the candidate 𝑦𝑖. With its default confidence threshold (𝜏=0.95), however, it commits only 3.0 tokens per block on average. Lowering the threshold commits more tokens, but also increases the frequency of committing token that diverges from greedy AR decoding. The proposed block therefore contains useful tokens that cannot be recovered simply by relaxing the free confidence rule. For an additional verifier pass to be worthwhile, it must identify enough of this unused matching prefix to compensate for its own latency. The verifier provides an additional signal. Given the context and proposed block 𝑦1, . . . , 𝑦𝐵, an AR verifier 𝑉 assigns each proposed token the probability 𝑞𝑖 = 𝑃𝑉 (𝑦𝑖 𝑥 𝑡, 𝑦1, . . . , 𝑦𝑖 1) , 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝐵. (2) All 𝐵 scores are obtained in one teacher-forced forward pass. Unlike the proposers confidence, which is computed from placeholders, the verifier scores each token after reading the actual prefix. The two scores, 𝑝𝑖 and 𝑞𝑖, answer different questions. The proposer confidence 𝑝𝑖 asks whether 𝑦𝑖 is plausible at that future position before the intervening future tokens have been instantiated. The verifier 4 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

Right: committed tokens per block against the fraction of blocks in which the gate commits non-matching token as each scores threshold is swept. probability 𝑞𝑖 asks whether the same token remains plausible after the concrete proposed prefix 𝑦<𝑖 has been revealed. Conceptually, 𝑝𝑖 plays prior-like role by exposing the proposers own preference, while 𝑞𝑖 is trajectory-conditioned on the proposal that actually materialized. token can therefore look plausible to the proposer in advance yet become inconsistent with the particular trajectory proposed before it. This also explains why the verifier can be much smaller than the proposer. The proposer must be capable of predicting several future positions while the intervening tokens remain unknown, whereas the verifier receives those tokens through teacher forcing. The verifier is not asked to reproduce the proposers longhorizon prediction ability; it only judges whether proposed continuation remains locally plausible after the missing context has been filled in. The proposer confidence is still useful because it records how strongly the proposer itself preferred the candidate. We therefore treat 𝑝𝑖 𝑞𝑖 as simple agreement score: it is high only when the candidate is both strongly supported by the proposer and compatible with the realized proposed prefix according to the verifier. Figure 4 compares the two signals and their product on the same proposed blocks. Verifier probability separates AR-matching from non-matching proposals better than proposer confidence, with AUC 0.960 versus 0.910. Their product reaches an AUC of 0.964 and performs comparably to the best hand-designed combinations we tested. Because the product is simple and parameter-free, we use it as the gate score in ProVe.

sections.title: 3.2 Verification
sections.content: ProVe decodes in repeated proposeverify cycles. Given the current context, the proposer first generates block of 𝐵 candidate tokens in one forward pass. The verifier then reads the context together with the proposed block in one teacher-forced pass. prefix of the proposed block is committed, and the next cycle starts from the extended context. There are two ways to verify the proposed block. ProVe: smaller model verifies. Let 𝑝𝑖 be the proposers confidence in its 𝑖-th proposed token and 𝑞𝑖 the verifier probability from Equation 2. We score each proposed token by their product, 𝑝𝑖 𝑞𝑖. For threshold 𝜃 , we commit the longest leading prefix whose tokens pass the threshold: 𝑎 = max {𝑡 {1, . . . , 𝐵} : 𝑝𝑖 𝑞𝑖 𝜃 for all 2 𝑖 𝑡 } . sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: from greedy AR decoding. The verifier never generates tokens itself. It only decides where to cut the proposed block. ProVe-lossless: the proposer verifies itself. special case is to use the proposer as its own verifier. After proposing block, we feed the proposed tokens back to the proposer as ordinary tokens in second forward pass. This pass gives the proposers greedy next-token prediction after every proposed prefix. We compare the proposal with these predictions from left to right. As long as they agree, the proposed prefix is exactly the prefix that ordinary greedy AR decoding would have produced. At the first disagreement, we commit the proposers greedy prediction instead and end the cycle. If all 𝐵 proposed tokens agree, we additionally commit the next greedy token produced after the full block. Every token committed by the cycle therefore lies on the proposers greedy AR trajectory. This gives simple induction argument for exactness: if the context at the start of cycle is greedy-AR prefix, matching proposed tokens keep the decoder on that same prefix, and the first disagreement is replaced by exactly the greedy next token. If the whole block matches, the token predicted after the full block is again the next greedy token. Repeating the argument across cycles reproduces the proposers greedy AR decoding token for token. ProVe-lossless therefore requires no threshold and no second model; each cycle consists of exactly two proposer forward passes.

sections.content: The advantage of reversing the two roles comes from where the serial work is paid. Let 𝑐𝑃 and 𝑐𝑉 denote the cost of one proposer and verifier pass, respectively, and define 𝜌 = 𝑐𝑉 /𝑐𝑃 . Normalizing one proposer pass to unit cost, the per-cycle costs 𝐶 are 𝐶ProVe = 1 + 𝜌, 𝐶ProVe-lossless = 2, 𝐶Spec = 1 + 𝑘𝜌, (4) where speculative decoding uses the same small model for 𝑘 serial drafting steps. If cycle commits 𝑎 tokens, its idealized speedup over ordinary AR decoding is 𝑎/𝐶. The key difference is the factor multiplying 𝜌. Speculative decoding invokes the small draft model 𝑘 times per cycle, whereas ProVe invokes the verifier only once. Increasing the proposal block size can expose more candidate tokens without adding another serial model call. larger verifier can therefore be affordable in regimes where using the same model for 𝑘 serial draft steps is not. For example, the 3B model in our implementation has 𝜌 0.34. The idealized per-cycle cost is then about 1.34 proposer-pass equivalents for ProVe, but 1 + 5𝜌 2.70 when the same model is used for five serial speculative-drafting steps. The small model has not become cheaper; its cost is simply paid once per proposed block rather than once per serial draft step. Actual speedup also depends on how many tokens each method commits per cycle. Equation 4 ignores the small additional cost of processing block and serving overheads. Measured pass costs and implementation details are given in Appendix A.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: There are three decoding rules making different use of the same block proposer. MARS uses one proposer pass and decides how far to proceed from the proposers placeholder-based confidence alone. ProVe adds one pass of smaller model that reads the realized proposed block, yielding tunable speedaccuracy tradeoff. ProVe-lossless instead spends second proposer pass to recover the exact greedy AR trajectory. The experiments below evaluate whether the extra verification pass pays for itself in throughput, and how the choice of verifier changes the resulting operating point. 6 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Setup. Our main proposer is Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2024), adapted into block-proposing AR model with 𝐵 = 16 following MARS (Jin et al., 2026). To isolate the incremental effect of block training, we use two-stage controlled pipeline: one epoch of ordinary AR SFT on the same instruction data, followed by one epoch of block-proposal training. The stage-1 AR checkpoint is control rather than requirement of ProVe; in practice, block training can continue from an already post-trained checkpoint using matched in-domain or post-training data. We use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and 7B-Instruct as verifiers, either as stock checkpoints or fine-tuned on generations from the proposer. Appendix reports training details and the effect of block training on ordinary AR quality. Baselines. We compare against five decoding baselines: standard autoregressive (AR) decoding, ProVelossless, the original MARS confidence rule, EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025a), and standard speculative decoding. AR performs ordinary greedy decoding with the same fine-tuned 32B model used as the proposer in our method, without block prediction or verification. We use it as the reference point for both task accuracy and decoding throughput. For ProVe, we evaluate confidence thresholds 𝜃 {0.10, 0.05, 0.01}, where 𝜃 is applied to the combined confidence score 𝑝𝑖 𝑞𝑖. The original MARS confidence rule serves as no-extra-pass control: it uses the same proposer and produces the same candidate blocks as ProVe, but directly commits the proposed tokens without an additional verification pass. For EAGLE-3, we used both its publicly released draft head and draft head fine-tuned specifically for our 32B proposer. Finally, we evaluate standard speculative decoding using the same stock 3B or 7B model as serial draft model, with the 32B model serving as the verifier. This provides controlled comparison in which the small model is held fixed while its role is reversed relative to our setup. We use speculative draft lengths 𝑘 {3, 5} and report sensitivity to 𝑘 in Appendix A. All methods use greedy decoding. Evaluation. We evaluate on the full test splits of HumanEval, GSM8K, GPQA, BBH, MMLU-Pro, and IFEval using the lm-evaluation-harness (Gao et al., 2024), with up to 1024 generated tokens. These benchmarks span short constrained outputs and substantially longer structured continuations, which is useful because block-decoding speed depends on how long proposed continuation remains predictable. Accuracy and throughput are measured from the same generations. All methods run in the same SGLang-based serving stack (Zheng et al., 2024), with single request in flight and the 32B proposer tensor-parallelized over two GPUs. Each configuration is compared with its own same-node AR run, and we report throughput relative to that reference. Additional serving details and evaluation uncertainty are given in Appendices and D.

sections.title: 4.1 Main results
sections.content: ProVe-lossless provides strong exact acceleration. Table 1 shows that ProVe-lossless reaches 2.54 AR throughput on average while reproducing the proposers greedy AR decoding. The speedup ranges from 1.43 on IFEval to 3.98 on BBH. The wide range already suggests that acceleration is controlled by the structure of the generated continuation rather than by fixed model-side speedup; Figure 6 returns to this variation below. ProVe-lossless requires neither second model nor separately trained draft head. For comparison, the public EAGLE-3 tree reaches 2.32 on average, while an EAGLE-3 head fine-tuned specifically for our proposer reaches 2.58. Thus, self-verification provides acceleration comparable to an external draft head tahat explicitly trained on proposers output. ProVe trades accuracy for additional speed. Using smaller verifier introduces controllable speed accuracy tradeoff through the threshold 𝜃 (Figure 5). With the stock 7B verifier at 𝜃 = 0.05, ProVe reaches 2.30 average throughput at only 0.3 points relative to AR. Lowering the threshold commits longer prefixes and increases speed: with stock 3B verifier at 𝜃 = 0.01, ProVe reaches 2.72 average throughput 7 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

Fine-tuning the verifier improves acceptance efficiency. Fine-tuning the verifier on generations from the proposer changes not only its ranking of proposed tokens but also the scale of its probabilities. fixed value of 𝜃 can therefore correspond to different levels of conservativeness before and after fine-tuning. To separate ranking quality from this calibration shift, we compare stock and trained verifiers at matched rates of committing non-matching token. At matched error rates, the fine-tuned verifiers commit 610% more tokens per cycle than their stock counterparts. We provide the full comparison in Appendix C. ProVe avoids serial drafting cost. At the conservative 𝜃 = 0.10 operating point, ProVe is faster than speculative decoding with the same small model. With the stock 3B model, speculative decoding reaches 1.63 average throughput, while ProVe reaches 2.28 at 1.2 points relative to AR. With the stock 7B model, the corresponding throughputs are 1.39 and 2.19, with ProVe at 0.6 points. Sweeping the speculative draft length over 𝑘 {3, 5} does not change this comparison; Appendix reports the full sensitivity. The difference is largest on longer structured generations such as BBH and GSM8K. This matches the cost analysis in Section 3.3: speculative decoding calls the small model repeatedly to draft tokens, whereas ProVe calls it once to verify one proposed block. Longer responses are usually faster. Figure 6 shows that the speedup tracks how much of proposed block can be committed. Across the 27 BBH subtasks, ProVe-lossless speedup increases from about 1.9 on the shortest responses to 5.5 on the longest, with correlation of 𝑟 = 0.59 with log response length. The same mechanism appears within individual GSM8K responses: the average AR-matching prefix grows from 4.2 tokens near the beginning of response to 8.9 tokens near the end, while ProVe-lossless commits 4.4 to 7.5 tokens per cycle. The method therefore benefits most when the continuation becomes predictable enough for single proposal to match greedy AR for several positions.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Speculative decoding and draft heads. Speculative decoding drafts 𝑘 tokens with cheap model and verifies them with the target in one pass, preserving the target distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023); later work cuts the draft cost with heads trained on the targets hidden states and tree-structured candidates (Li et al., 2024a;b; 2025a), the targets own early layers (Zhang et al., 2024; Elhoushi et al., 2024), Jacobi-style 𝑛-gram candidates (Fu et al., 2024) or of suffix automaton (Hu et al., 2025). Nearly all of this work is exact, the draft only changes speed, and the roles are fixed: drafter are designed to be small and cheap, while the verifier are large and expensive. Judge Decoding (Bachmann et al., 2025) and Big Little Decoder (Kim et al., 2023) relax the verifiers rule, as ProVe does with its threshold. Neither lets the large model propose. Block proposals. Several methods let model propose several positions in one of its own passes: PaSS (Monea et al., 2023) appends learned look-ahead embeddings, Parallel Prompt Decoding (Chen et al., 2025) trained prompt tokens, Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) extra heads, multi-token prediction (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024) extra output modules, and Set Block Decoding (Gat et al., 2025) and MARS (Jin et al., 2026) fine-tune the model to predict masked future tokens, the proposer of this paper. ReDrafter (Cheng et al., 2024), Amphista (Li et al., 2025b), FastEagle (Huang et al., 2025) and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) draft block in one pass of trained small draft network under exact verification by the target, the standard direction with block draft; IDLM (Yu et al., 2026) fuses the verification of one proposed block and the proposal of the next into one pass of the same model. Block diffusion models (Arriola et al., 2025), DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026) and MARS commit on the models own confidence; what ProVe adds is the verifying pass that reads the proposed block. And through experiments, we show that the verification step is essential to commit more tokens. 10 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we show that block proposals contain substantially more usable content than the proposers own confidence suggests: on GSM8K, the proposed block has an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens, while the original confidence rule commits only 3.0. The gap arises because proposer confidence is computed from placeholders and therefore does not see the realized proposed prefix. verifier instead reads the proposed tokens themselves, providing second signal for deciding how much of the block to commit. This simple change gives ProVe two useful operating alternatives. With smaller verifier, ProVe provides controllable speedaccuracy tradeoff; when the proposer verifies itself, ProVe-lossless reproduces greedy AR decoding with no second model and reaches 2.5 average AR throughput. Our results suggest that block proposal and verification need not follow the traditional speculative-decoding division of labor. large model can propose several tokens in parallel, while verification can be performed in one additional pass.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: Serving. All configurations run in one SGLang-based stack (Zheng et al., 2024) extended with the ProVe algorithms, on two data-center GPUs with tensor parallelism of two for the 32B model, bf16 weights, the FlashInfer attention backend and single request in flight; the AR controls use the unmodified server. ProVe is decoding algorithm with small configuration: block size 16, the product rule of Equation 3 with its threshold, the verifier checkpoint and the fraction of device memory reserved for the in-process verifier (its weights, KV cache and CUDA graphs): 0.18 for the 3B and 0.32 for the 7B, with the proposers static pool at 0.70 and 0.55 so that the two never compete (an undersized verifier pool does not fail but silently degrades toward one accepted token per cycle; Appendix D). Each cycle is one scheduler step per pass, and proposed tokens that are not committed are dropped from the proposers KV cache before the next cycle, so the cache after cycle equals what AR decoding of the committed context would have produced. Spec uses the stacks standalone-draft implementation with the same 3B or 7B checkpoint; we evaluate serial draft lengths 𝑘 {3, 5} and report the sweep below. EAGLE-3 uses the stacks implementation with the head as chain of five draft steps and with its default tree of 60 draft tokens  (Table 1)  . Measured pass costs. On the same two GPUs (60 GSM8K problems): one AR decode step 14.8 ms; one pass of the 32B over 16-token window 15.6 ms, both as the proposing and as the verifying pass of ProVe-lossless; one in-process pass of the 3B verifier 5.0 ms (𝜌 = 0.34) and of the 7B 5.8 ms (𝜌 = 0.40). The verifiers pass is dominated by fixed per-call cost of about 2.7 ms that does not depend on its size (the 0.5B costs 3.0 ms, halving the 7Bs weight bytes with fp8 saves 0.2 ms, and running it without tensor parallelism is slower, 6.9 ms), which is why stronger verifier is nearly free in Equation 4. Per-cycle scheduling and cache-trimming overhead is 8.7 ms in ProVe-lossless and 4 ms in ProVe, the part the equation omits; with it, 7.27/(2 1.05 + 0.59) = 2.70 against the measured 2.70 for ProVe-lossless, and 4.13/(1.05 + 0.34 + 0.27) = 2.49 against 2.49 for ProVe with the 3B verifier at 𝜃 = 0.10. Block size. The proposer was trained with 16 placeholders but proposes longer block when asked. On the full GSM8K test set ProVe-lossless commits 5.9 / 7.5 / 8.1 / 8.6 tokens per cycle at 𝐵 = 8/16/24/32 and decodes at 2.44/2.79/2.84/2.84: the speedup saturates from 𝐵 = 24 on because both passes pay for every row of the window, and every other experiment uses the 𝐵 = 16 the proposer was trained with. Both proposers use the reference implementation of Jin et al. (2026) on 32 GPUs: the instruction proposer 150 GPU hours for the AR stage and 384 for the block stage at 512 tokens per stream; the reasoning proposer 1,194 GPU hours at 16k tokens, single-benchmark check because reasoning traces are long and block training doubles every sequence. sections.title: D Measurement Validity
sections.content: Exactness of ProVe-lossless. Feeding each generation of the main campaign back to the plain AR server with per-token log probabilities, the tokens of ProVe-lossless are the argmax at every position except 0.84%, against 0.85% for the AR servers own generations scored the same way, with the same distribution of gaps to the argmax (median 0, maximum 0.4 nats): the two decoders differ only in bf16 tie-breaking. On the reasoning line the generations are long enough for tie-breaking to show: over 300 GSM8K problems, 20 generations are identical token for token, the first differing token sits at median position of 176, and 266 of the 280 diverged pairs end at the same final answer. Repeats and pooling. Repeats of the same configuration on different nodes agree in accuracy to the item and in throughput within 2%, except at the loosest thresholds of the 3B and 7B verifiers, which moved by 8 16 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

sections.content: to 10% in opposite directions; every comparison in the paper is therefore decoded on one node in one job with its own AR run. Throughput is total generated tokens over total in-flight seconds of unit; averaging per-request rates would overweight short generations, whose rate is dominated by prefill and the first cycle. Evaluation uncertainty. We evaluate all methods on the full evaluation split of each benchmark. The test-set sizes and corresponding 95% confidence half-widths for the main six-benchmark evaluation are: HumanEval, 𝑛 = 164 (5.9 points); GSM8K, 𝑛 = 1319 (1.7); GPQA, 𝑛 = 448 (4.4); BBH, 𝑛 = 6511 (0.9); MMLU-Pro, 𝑛 = 12032 (0.9); and IFEval, 𝑛 = 541 (3.2). We therefore do not interpret accuracy differences within these ranges as meaningful differences between decoding methods. For the reasoningmodel evaluation, MATH-500 contains 500 problems and has 95% confidence half-width of approximately 2.4 points, which covers the accuracy differences among the configurations we report. silent failure. An undersized in-process verifier pool does not fail but degrades ProVe toward one accepted token per cycle; with the 7B verifier fraction of 0.25 starved the pool (probe 119 instead of 172 tok/s) and the campaign uses 0.32 with the proposers pool at 0.55. Concurrency. Each ProVe cycle occupies more accelerator rows per accepted token than AR decoding, free only while the device is latency bound, so the advantage narrows with the number of concurrent requests 𝐶 (Figure 8). On GSM8K prompts, throughput relative to AR at the same 𝐶 falls from 3.2 at 𝐶 = 1 to 2.4 at 𝐶 = 8 and 1.6 at 𝐶 = 32 for ProVe-lossless, and from 3.3 to 2.3 and 1.3 for ProVe (stock 3B verifier, 𝜃 = 0.01), ahead of ProVe-lossless up to 𝐶 = 4 and behind it from 𝐶 = 8 on; the EAGLE-3 tree, at 60 rows per cycle, falls from 3.5 to 1.9 and reaches AR at 𝐶 = 32. Figure 8. System throughput against the number of concurrent requests 𝐶 on GSM8K prompts (up to 512 new tokens, about 140 generated per request), 32B instruction proposer, one two-GPU server per decoder, all four decoders on the same node. Left: generated tokens per second over all requests in flight; right: the same relative to AR at the same 𝐶.

sections.title: E Limitations
sections.content: Proposer training. The proposer requires block-specific fine-tuning and is therefore not drop-in accelerator for an arbitrary checkpoint. Our proposer is also substantially under-trained relative to the original MARS recipe because of our compute budget. MARS uses five epochs of ordinary AR training followed by five epochs of block training, whereas we use only one epoch of each, or 20% of the training in each stage. Despite this limited training, our proposer already produces an average AR-matching prefix of 6.6 tokens on GSM8K. More training data, longer block training, or incorporating the block-proposal 17 ProVe: Proposer-Verifier Decoding

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: objective during pretraining could substantially improve proposal quality and, consequently, the speedups of both ProVe variants. Serving implementation. Our implementation is research-oriented and remains less optimized than industrial inference systems. The current serving stack incurs fixed overheads from scheduling, KV-cache management, and verifier calls that are not intrinsic to proposer-verifier decoding. These overheads reduce the realized speedup, particularly under concurrency. production implementation with more tightly integrated proposeverify loop, optimized cache management, and lower per-call overhead could translate longer committed prefixes more directly into end-to-end throughput. Greedy decoding only. All reported experiments use greedy decoding. ProVe-lossless can in principle be extended to sampling using speculative-sampling correction that preserves the target distribution, but we have not implemented or evaluated this setting in our serving system. The behavior and efficiency of ProVe under sampling therefore remain to be studied. ProVe is not distribution-exact. Unlike ProVe-lossless, ProVe with smaller verifier uses thresholded acceptance rule and does not preserve the proposers greedy AR output exactly. Its speedaccuracy tradeoff therefore depends on the verifier, threshold, and task, and we do not extrapolate the measured accuracy effects beyond the settings evaluated in this work. Scope. Our experiments cover one model family (Qwen) and one proposer scale (32B). The instruction proposer is evaluated on six benchmarks, while the reasoning proposer is evaluated on GSM8K and MATH500. Whether the same gains hold across substantially different model families and scales remains an open question.
